title: Immunology
summary: Innate and adaptive defences, antibodies, vaccines and disorders.

layers.basics: The immune system recognises and removes threats. Innate defences respond fast and generally; adaptive defences respond specifically and remember.
layers.deeper: Barriers, phagocytes and inflammation form the first response. B and T lymphocytes recognise specific antigens, make antibodies and kill infected cells, and memory cells give lasting protection after infection or vaccination.
layers.expert: Immune responses balance defence and tolerance. Failures cause allergy, autoimmunity or immunodeficiency; manipulating them underlies vaccines, transplants and cancer immunotherapy. Each lymphocyte carries a receptor made by random gene rearrangement; selection in the thymus and bone marrow, regulatory T cells and checkpoint receptors keep self-reactive cells in check, and when this balance fails, disease results.

title: Innate immunity: barriers, phagocytes and inflammation

layers.basics: Skin, mucus and acid block most invaders. Phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages) engulf microbes and inflammation brings more cells.
layers.deeper: Complement proteins mark and kill microbes; interferons warn neighbouring cells about viruses; fever raises body temperature, which slows the growth of many microbes and boosts innate defences, though too high a fever damages tissue.
layers.expert: Pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like receptors) detect PAMPs. NF-κB drives cytokine release; neutrophil extracellular traps catch microbes. Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

facts: the most abundant white blood cell type

title: MHC and antigen presentation

layers.basics: Cells display protein fragments on MHC molecules. T cells check these fragments to decide whether a cell is infected or foreign.
layers.deeper: MHC I (on all nucleated cells) presents to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells; MHC II (on dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) presents to CD4⁺ helper T cells. Dendritic cells can also load antigen taken up from outside onto MHC I (cross-presentation) to prime CD8⁺ T cells.
layers.expert: HLA genes are the most polymorphic in humans (about 46,000 named alleles, still rising). Matching HLA is key for transplants. The thymus keeps T cells that recognise self-MHC with modest affinity and deletes those that bind self-peptide–MHC too strongly. The deletion is imperfect, so some self-reactive cells escape and are held in check by peripheral tolerance.

facts: short peptides, mostly 8–11 aa (MHC class II binds longer ones, about 13–25 aa)

layers.basics: Helper T cells coordinate other immune cells; cytotoxic T cells kill infected or cancerous cells.
layers.deeper: Naive T cells activate in lymph nodes after meeting antigen with co-stimulation, then multiply enormously; CD8⁺ T cells in a strong acute infection can expand many thousand-fold, while CD4⁺ cells expand less.
layers.expert: T cell receptors are generated by V(D)J recombination (in principle 10¹⁵ to 10²⁰ different receptors are possible, but one person carries far fewer distinct clonotypes; estimates range from about 10⁶ to 10⁸ and depend on the method). Regulatory T cells enforce tolerance; checkpoint receptors (PD-1, CTLA-4) restrain responses.

title: B cells and antibodies

layers.basics: B cells make antibodies that bind antigens, marking them for destruction or neutralising them.
layers.deeper: Antibody classes: IgM (first made), IgG (most abundant in blood), IgA (in mucosal secretions), IgE (allergy, parasites), IgD (mainly a B-cell surface receptor; its role is less clear). Plasma cells secrete very large numbers of antibodies.
layers.expert: Antibodies are Y-shaped with two heavy and two light chains; variable regions give specificity. Somatic hypermutation in germinal centres, with selection of the best binders, raises antibody affinity over the course of a response; class switching changes the antibody class and can also occur outside germinal centres.

facts: very many per second (rate depends on cell type and method)

title: Antibody and receptor diversity (V(D)J)
summary: Generating a vast repertoire from few genes.

layers.basics: Gene segments are cut and pasted in developing lymphocytes to make a unique receptor in each cell.
layers.deeper: RAG1/2 enzymes drive the rearrangement. Junctional diversity and hypermutation add more variation.
layers.expert: The theoretical repertoire is enormous (estimates vary widely with what is counted), but any one person has far fewer distinct antibodies at one time. Tonegawa received the 1987 Nobel for explaining this. Immune repertoire sequencing now tracks clones during disease and vaccination.

facts: vast (theoretical estimates vary; one person has far fewer)

steps.title: Recognition
steps.text: RAG1 and RAG2 proteins bind recombination signal sequences that flank the V, D and J gene segments.

steps.title: Cutting
steps.text: RAG cuts the DNA at two chosen segments, leaving hairpin-sealed ends.

steps.title: Trimming and adding
steps.text: Nucleases trim the ends and the enzyme TdT adds random nucleotides, which makes each junction different.

steps.title: Joining
steps.text: Non-homologous end joining repairs the break and ligates the segments into one gene exon.

steps.title: A unique receptor
steps.text: Each developing lymphocyte ends up with its own combination, so each cell makes a receptor with its own binding site.

title: Clonal selection and immune memory

layers.basics: When an antigen meets the matching lymphocyte it multiplies. After infection some cells remain as memory cells.
layers.deeper: Primary responses start slowly and build over days to weeks; secondary responses start sooner, rise faster and reach far higher antibody levels.
layers.expert: Burnet's clonal selection theory (1957) is a cornerstone of immunology. Memory B-cell and long-lived plasma cell pools can last for years to decades for some antigens; some antigens (influenza) drift and evade memory.

open_questions: Why does immune memory last decades for some infections and vaccines but fade within months to years for others?

layers.basics: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form of a pathogen so it builds memory. Types include live-attenuated, inactivated, subunit and mRNA vaccines.
layers.deeper: Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a global campaign of vaccination and surveillance. When enough people are immune, outbreaks fade; the herd immunity threshold is ≈ 1 − 1/R₀ if people mix randomly and the vaccine fully protects everyone it reaches. Lower vaccine efficacy or uneven mixing raises the coverage needed.
layers.expert: Adjuvants boost responses; mRNA-LNP vaccines encode antigens and were deployed in 2020–21 (Nobel 2023 for nucleoside modification). Vaccine effectiveness is evaluated by randomised trials and observational data; waning immunity and escape require boosters.

title: Allergy and autoimmunity

layers.basics: Allergies are overreactions to harmless substances, driven by IgE. In autoimmune disease the body attacks its own tissues, as in type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.
layers.deeper: Gell–Coombs types I–IV classify hypersensitivity. Anaphylaxis can be life threatening and is treated with adrenaline.
layers.expert: Autoimmune diseases together affect a few percent of people; estimates differ by country and by which diseases are counted. Most are more common in women, though not all. Triggers combine genes (HLA), infection and environment; molecular mimicry is one proposed mechanism.

facts: a few percent (estimates vary with which diseases are counted)
open_questions: What triggers autoimmune disease in people who carry risk genes?
How often does molecular mimicry cause disease rather than merely coincide with it?
Why has the prevalence of allergy and some autoimmune diseases risen in recent decades?

title: Immunodeficiency, transplantation and tolerance

layers.basics: Immunodeficiency can be inherited or acquired (HIV). Transplants are rejected unless donors are matched and immune responses are suppressed.
layers.deeper: Tolerance means not attacking self. Immunosuppressive drugs like cyclosporine prevent rejection but raise infection risk.
layers.expert: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID, the "bubble boy" disease) was among the first diseases treated by gene therapy. Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor T cells attack the recipient. Pregnancy shows that the immune system can tolerate a partly foreign fetus; several mechanisms (trophoblast cells with unusual MHC, regulatory T cells, local immune modulation) are proposed, and how they work together is not fully understood.

open_questions: How can transplant recipients be given lasting, specific tolerance without lifelong immunosuppression?
How is the fetus tolerated in pregnancy?

title: Cancer and immunotherapy

layers.basics: Immunotherapy removes brakes on T cells (checkpoint inhibitors) or engineers T cells to attack tumours (CAR-T).
layers.deeper: Allison and Honjo won the 2018 Nobel for checkpoint blockade. Responses can be durable in some melanoma and lung cancer patients.
layers.expert: Response rates vary widely between tumour types and are low in many; one upper-bound analysis estimated that about 12% of US patients with cancer would respond to a checkpoint inhibitor in 2018. Biomarkers include PD-L1 and tumour mutational burden. Side effects include immune-related adverse events.

open_questions: Why do some tumours respond durably and others not at all, and which biomarkers predict it?
How can immune-related side effects be separated from anti-tumour effects?
Can CAR-T work in solid tumours?

layers.basics: ELISA uses an enzyme-linked antibody to produce a colour change that tells how much antigen is present.
layers.deeper: Lateral-flow tests (pregnancy, rapid antigen) use antibodies on a strip. Flow cytometry counts and sorts cells by fluorescent antibody labels.
layers.expert: Sandwich ELISA can detect very low concentrations, often in the pg/mL to ng/mL range depending on the antibody pair and the analyte. Monoclonal antibodies (Köhler and Milstein, 1975) provide specificity. Controls and standard curves are essential for quantitation.
